cards.q: What is an electric field?
cards.a: A region in which a charged particle experiences a force.

cards.q: Define electric field strength at a point, and state its direction.
cards.a: The force per unit positive charge at that point: E=FQ\displaystyle E = \frac{F}{Q}E=QF​. Its direction is the direction of the force on a positive charge. Unit: N C−1\displaystyle \text{N C}^{-1}N C−1.

cards.q: State Coulomb's law.
cards.a: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: F=14πε0Q1Q2r2\displaystyle F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{r^{2}}F=4πε0​1​r2Q1​Q2​​.
cards.why: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

cards.q: Two point charges of 2.0 μC\displaystyle 2.0\ \mu\text{C}2.0 μC each are 0.30 m apart in air. Calculate the force between them. (14πε0=8.99×109 N m2 C−2\displaystyle \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}4πε0​1​=8.99×109 N m2 C−2)
cards.a: 0.40 N
cards.why: Forgetting to square the separation is the most common slip.
steps: Convert: 2.0 μC=2.0×10−6 C\displaystyle 2.0\ \mu\text{C} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C}2.0 μC=2.0×10−6 C.
F=8.99×109×(2.0×10−6)20.302\displaystyle F = \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9} \times (2.0 \times 10^{-6})^{2}}{0.30^{2}}F=0.3028.99×109×(2.0×10−6)2​
F=0.40 N\displaystyle F = 0.40\ \text{N}F=0.40 N

cards.q: When using Coulomb's law for a charged sphere in air, what two simplifications are made?
cards.a: The charge on the sphere is treated as if it were all at the centre, and air is treated as a vacuum.

cards.q: Calculate the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between two protons. cards.why: Gravity is negligible between subatomic particles.

cards.q: Write the equation for the electric field strength between two parallel plates.
cards.a: E=Vd\displaystyle E = \frac{V}{d}E=dV​, where V\displaystyle VV is the potential difference between the plates and d\displaystyle dd their separation. Unit: V m−1\displaystyle \text{V m}^{-1}V m−1.
cards.why: The field between the plates is uniform: the same everywhere.

cards.q: Derive E=Vd\displaystyle E = \frac{V}{d}E=dV​ for a uniform field by considering the work done moving a charge Q\displaystyle QQ between the plates.
cards.a: E=Vd\displaystyle E = \frac{V}{d}E=dV​
steps: Work done moving the charge across is force × distance: W=Fd\displaystyle W = FdW=Fd.
It is also charge × potential difference: W=QV\displaystyle W = QVW=QV.
So Fd=QV\displaystyle Fd = QVFd=QV, and FQ=Vd\displaystyle \frac{F}{Q} = \frac{V}{d}QF​=dV​.
FQ\displaystyle \frac{F}{Q}QF​ is the field strength, so E=Vd\displaystyle E = \frac{V}{d}E=dV​.

cards.q: A potential difference of 500 V is applied across parallel plates 0.020 m apart. Calculate the field strength between them.
cards.a: 2.5×104 V m−1\displaystyle 2.5 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}2.5×104 V m−1
steps: E=Vd=5000.020\displaystyle E = \frac{V}{d} = \frac{500}{0.020}E=dV​=0.020500​
E=2.5×104 V m−1\displaystyle E = 2.5 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}E=2.5×104 V m−1

cards.q: Calculate the force on an electron in a uniform field of strength 2.5×104 V m−1\displaystyle 2.5 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}2.5×104 V m−1. (e=1.60×10−19 C\displaystyle e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}e=1.60×10−19 C)
cards.a: 4.0×10−15 N\displaystyle 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{N}4.0×10−15 N
cards.why: The force on an electron is opposite to the field direction, because its charge is negative.
steps: F=EQ=2.5×104×1.60×10−19\displaystyle F = EQ = 2.5 \times 10^{4} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}F=EQ=2.5×104×1.60×10−19
F=4.0×10−15 N\displaystyle F = 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{N}F=4.0×10−15 N

cards.q: A charged particle enters a uniform electric field at right angles to the field. Describe its path, and explain why.
cards.a: A parabola. Its velocity along its original direction is constant, while it has a constant acceleration in the direction of the force, just like a projectile under gravity.

cards.q: Write the equation for the electric field strength at a distance r\displaystyle rr from a point charge Q\displaystyle QQ.
cards.a: E=14πε0Qr2\displaystyle E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r^{2}}E=4πε0​1​r2Q​

cards.q: Calculate the electric field strength 0.10 m from a point charge of 5.0 nC. (14πε0=8.99×109 N m2 C−2\displaystyle \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}4πε0​1​=8.99×109 N m2 C−2)
cards.a: 4.5×103 N C−1\displaystyle 4.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N C}^{-1}4.5×103 N C−1
steps: Convert: 5.0 nC=5.0×10−9 C\displaystyle 5.0\ \text{nC} = 5.0 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C}5.0 nC=5.0×10−9 C.
E=8.99×109×5.0×10−90.102\displaystyle E = \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.10^{2}}E=0.1028.99×109×5.0×10−9​
E=4.5×103 N C−1\displaystyle E = 4.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N C}^{-1}E=4.5×103 N C−1

cards.q: Describe the electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge, and between two oppositely charged parallel plates.
cards.a: Point charge: radial, pointing away from the charge. Parallel plates: parallel and equally spaced, from the positive plate to the negative plate.
cards.why: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge.

cards.q: Define electric potential at a point.
cards.a: The work done per unit positive charge in moving a small positive charge from infinity to that point. Unit: V (J C−1\displaystyle \text{J C}^{-1}J C−1).

cards.q: Write the equation for the electric potential at a distance r\displaystyle rr from a point charge Q\displaystyle QQ.
cards.a: V=14πε0Qr\displaystyle V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}V=4πε0​1​rQ​
cards.why: The sign of the potential follows the sign of the charge: positive near a positive charge, negative near a negative one.

cards.q: Calculate the electric potential 0.10 m from a point charge of 5.0 nC. (14πε0=8.99×109 N m2 C−2\displaystyle \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}4πε0​1​=8.99×109 N m2 C−2)
cards.a: 450 V
cards.why: Potential uses r\displaystyle rr, not r2\displaystyle r^{2}r2.
steps: V=8.99×109×5.0×10−90.10\displaystyle V = \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.10}V=0.108.99×109×5.0×10−9​
V=450 V\displaystyle V = 450\ \text{V}V=450 V

cards.q: How much work is done moving a charge Q\displaystyle QQ through a potential difference ΔV\displaystyle \Delta VΔV?
cards.a: ΔW=QΔV\displaystyle \Delta W = Q\Delta VΔW=QΔV
cards.why: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential, where ΔV=0\displaystyle \Delta V = 0ΔV=0.

cards.q: How is electric field strength related to the way potential changes with distance?
cards.a: Field strength is the potential gradient: E=ΔVΔr\displaystyle E = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}E=ΔrΔV​ in magnitude, and the field points in the direction in which the potential falls.
cards.why: Where equipotentials are close together, the field is strong.

cards.q: What does the area under a graph of electric field strength E\displaystyle EE against distance r\displaystyle rr represent?
cards.a: The potential difference between the two distances.

cards.q: Define capacitance, and state its unit.
cards.a: The charge stored per unit potential difference: C=QV\displaystyle C = \frac{Q}{V}C=VQ​. Unit: the farad, F.

cards.q: A 470 μF\displaystyle 470\ \mu\text{F}470 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Calculate the charge stored.
cards.a: 5.6×10−3 C\displaystyle 5.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}5.6×10−3 C
steps: Convert: 470 μF=470×10−6 F\displaystyle 470\ \mu\text{F} = 470 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{F}470 μF=470×10−6 F.
Q=CV=470×10−6×12\displaystyle Q = CV = 470 \times 10^{-6} \times 12Q=CV=470×10−6×12
Q=5.6×10−3 C\displaystyle Q = 5.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}Q=5.6×10−3 C

cards.q: Write the equation for the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, and say what each symbol means.
cards.a: C=Aε0εrd\displaystyle C = \frac{A\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}}{d}C=dAε0​εr​​: A\displaystyle AA the area of overlap of the plates, d\displaystyle dd their separation, ε0\displaystyle \varepsilon_{0}ε0​ the permittivity of free space, εr\displaystyle \varepsilon_{r}εr​ the relative permittivity of the material between them.

cards.q: Two plates of area 0.020 m2\displaystyle 0.020\ \text{m}^{2}0.020 m2 are 1.0 mm apart in air. Calculate the capacitance. (ε0=8.85×10−12 F m−1\displaystyle \varepsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F m}^{-1}ε0​=8.85×10−12 F m−1; take εr=1\displaystyle \varepsilon_{r} = 1εr​=1)
cards.a: 1.8×10−10 F\displaystyle 1.8 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{F}1.8×10−10 F
steps: Convert: d=1.0×10−3 m\displaystyle d = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}d=1.0×10−3 m.

C=Aε0εrd=0.020×8.85×10−12×11.0×10−3\displaystyle C = \frac{A\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}}{d} = \frac{0.020 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 1}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}C=dAε0​εr​​=1.0×10−30.020×8.85×10−12×1​
C=1.8×10−10 F\displaystyle C = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{F}C=1.8×10−10 F

cards.q: What is the relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of a material?
cards.a: The factor by which the capacitance increases when the material completely fills the space between the plates, compared with a vacuum.

cards.q: Explain how a dielectric made of polar molecules increases the capacitance of a capacitor.
cards.a: Its molecules line up and set up a field that opposes the field between the plates.
marks: The polar molecules rotate in the electric field so that they line up with it.
Their charges produce an electric field in the opposite direction to the field between the plates.
This reduces the overall field, and so the potential difference, for the same charge on the plates.
C=QV\displaystyle C = \frac{Q}{V}C=VQ​: a smaller potential difference for the same charge means a larger capacitance.

cards.q: Write three equivalent expressions for the energy stored by a capacitor.
cards.a: E=12QV=12CV2=Q22C\displaystyle E = \frac{1}{2}QV = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \frac{Q^{2}}{2C}E=21​QV=21​CV2=2CQ2​

cards.q: Use the graph of potential difference against charge for a capacitor to show that the energy stored is 12QV\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}QV21​QV.
cards.a: W=12QV\displaystyle W = \frac{1}{2}QVW=21​QV
cards.why: The half is there because the potential difference rises from zero as the capacitor charges.
steps: V=QC\displaystyle V = \frac{Q}{C}V=CQ​, so the graph of V\displaystyle VV against Q\displaystyle QQ is a straight line through the origin.
The work done adding a small charge ΔQ\displaystyle \Delta QΔQ at potential difference V\displaystyle VV is VΔQ\displaystyle V\Delta QVΔQ: a thin strip of area under the graph.
The total work done is the whole area under the graph: a triangle.
Area =12×base×height=12QV\displaystyle = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}QV=21​×base×height=21​QV.

cards.q: Calculate the energy stored by a 470 μF\displaystyle 470\ \mu\text{F}470 μF capacitor charged to 12 V.
cards.a: 0.034 J
steps: E=12CV2=12×470×10−6×122\displaystyle E = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 470 \times 10^{-6} \times 12^{2}E=21​CV2=21​×470×10−6×122
E=0.034 J\displaystyle E = 0.034\ \text{J}E=0.034 J

cards.q: What is the time constant of a resistor–capacitor circuit?
cards.a: RC\displaystyle RCRC: the time taken for the charge (or the potential difference, or the current) of a discharging capacitor to fall to 1e\displaystyle \frac{1}{e}e1​, about 37%, of its initial value.

cards.q: A 470 μF\displaystyle 470\ \mu\text{F}470 μF capacitor discharges through a 10 kΩ\displaystyle 10\ \text{k}\Omega10 kΩ resistor. Calculate the time constant.
cards.a: 4.7 s
steps: Convert: R=10×103 Ω\displaystyle R = 10 \times 10^{3}\ \OmegaR=10×103 Ω, C=470×10−6 F\displaystyle C = 470 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{F}C=470×10−6 F.
RC=10×103×470×10−6\displaystyle RC = 10 \times 10^{3} \times 470 \times 10^{-6}RC=10×103×470×10−6
RC=4.7 s\displaystyle RC = 4.7\ \text{s}RC=4.7 s

cards.q: Write the equation for the charge on a capacitor discharging through a resistor. Which other quantities follow the same equation?
cards.a: Q=Q0e−tRC\displaystyle Q = Q_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}Q=Q0​e−RCt​. The potential difference and the current decay in the same way: V=V0e−tRC\displaystyle V = V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}V=V0​e−RCt​ and I=I0e−tRC\displaystyle I = I_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}I=I0​e−RCt​.

cards.q: A capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a resistor. The time constant is 4.7 s. Calculate the potential difference across it after 10 s.
cards.a: 1.4 V
steps: V=V0e−tRC=12×e−104.7\displaystyle V = V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} = 12 \times e^{-\frac{10}{4.7}}V=V0​e−RCt​=12×e−4.710​
e−2.13=0.119\displaystyle e^{-2.13} = 0.119e−2.13=0.119
V=12×0.119=1.4 V\displaystyle V = 12 \times 0.119 = 1.4\ \text{V}V=12×0.119=1.4 V

cards.q: A capacitor discharges with a time constant of 2.0 s. Calculate the time taken for its charge to fall to half its initial value.
cards.a: 1.4 s
cards.why: 0.69 is ln⁡2\displaystyle \ln 2ln2: setting Q=12Q0\displaystyle Q = \frac{1}{2}Q_{0}Q=21​Q0​ in the discharge equation gives t=RCln⁡2\displaystyle t = RC\ln 2t=RCln2.
steps: Time to halve: T12=0.69RC\displaystyle T_{\frac{1}{2}} = 0.69RCT21​​=0.69RC.
T12=0.69×2.0\displaystyle T_{\frac{1}{2}} = 0.69 \times 2.0T21​​=0.69×2.0
T12=1.4 s\displaystyle T_{\frac{1}{2}} = 1.4\ \text{s}T21​​=1.4 s

cards.q: Write the equation for the charge on a capacitor as it charges through a resistor.
cards.a: Q=Q0(1−e−tRC)\displaystyle Q = Q_{0}\left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\right)Q=Q0​(1−e−RCt​), where Q0\displaystyle Q_{0}Q0​ is the final charge.
cards.why: The potential difference across the capacitor rises in the same way. The current does not: it decays exponentially.

cards.q: A capacitor is charging through a resistor. A student writes the current as I=I0(1−e−tRC)\displaystyle I = I_{0}\left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\right)I=I0​(1−e−RCt​). What is wrong?
cards.a: While charging, the current decays from its initial value: I=I0e−tRC\displaystyle I = I_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}I=I0​e−RCt​. Only the charge and the potential difference across the capacitor follow the rising 1−e−tRC\displaystyle 1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}1−e−RCt​ form.

cards.q: Explain why the current falls as a capacitor charges through a resistor from a fixed supply.
cards.a: The growing potential difference across the capacitor leaves less across the resistor.
marks: As charge builds up on the plates, the potential difference across the capacitor rises.
The supply potential difference is shared between the capacitor and the resistor.
So the potential difference across the resistor falls.
I=VR\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​, so the current falls, reaching zero when the capacitor is fully charged.

cards.q: For a capacitor circuit, what does the gradient of a charge–time graph represent, and the area under a current–time graph?
cards.a: Gradient of charge–time: the current. Area under current–time: the charge that has flowed.

cards.q: For a discharging capacitor, what graph gives a straight line, and how is the time constant found from it?
cards.a: ln⁡V\displaystyle \ln VlnV against t\displaystyle tt. Its gradient is −1RC\displaystyle -\frac{1}{RC}−RC1​, so RC=−1gradient\displaystyle RC = -\frac{1}{\text{gradient}}RC=−gradient1​.

cards.q: Outline how to determine the time constant of a capacitor discharging through a resistor.
cards.a: Record the potential difference as the capacitor discharges and plot a log graph.
marks: Charge the capacitor from a supply, then switch it to discharge through a resistor.
Record the potential difference across the capacitor at regular times, with a data logger, an oscilloscope, or a voltmeter and stopwatch.
Plot ln⁡V\displaystyle \ln VlnV against t\displaystyle tt: a straight line.
The gradient is −1RC\displaystyle -\frac{1}{RC}−RC1​, so the time constant is −1gradient\displaystyle -\frac{1}{\text{gradient}}−gradient1​.

cards.q: After how many time constants is a discharging capacitor usually treated as fully discharged?
cards.a: About five: by then less than 1% of the initial charge remains.
cards.why: e−5=0.0067\displaystyle e^{-5} = 0.0067e−5=0.0067.
